proposal.reactor_type: Transparent PFA coil reactor wrapped around UV lamp (annular photoreactor)
proposal.residence_time_basis: Total combined stream volumetric flow rate through the illuminated coil volume
proposal.light_setup: 365 nm UV LED strip (or Hg lamp with 365 nm bandpass filter) mounted axially inside a cylindrical reflector; PFA coil wound tightly around the lamp housing; estimated irradiance at coil surface ~50 mW/cm²; lamp cooled by forced air to maintain reactor at 30 °C
proposal.mixer_type: T-mixer (PTFE, 0.5 mm bore) immediately upstream of the photoreactor coil
proposal.mixing_order_reasoning: S1 (substrate) and S2 (NBS) are combined at the T-mixer just before entering the illuminated zone. Pre-mixing in the dark is intentional: NBS is light-sensitive and radical chain initiation should begin only inside the photoreactor. Combining both streams at equal flow rates (0.2 + 0.2 = 0.4 mL/min total) gives a post-mix substrate concentration of 0.10 M and NBS concentration of 0.20 M (2.0 equiv), matching the batch stoichiometry. No gas stream is required because the reaction is a radical benzylic/alpha-C–H bromination driven by Br• generated photolytically from NBS; dissolved oxygen is not a co-reagent but should be minimised (see pre_reactor_steps).
pre_reactor_steps: Degas both CCl4 stock solutions by sparging with nitrogen for 15 min to remove dissolved O2, which can quench carbon radicals and reduce yield.
Prepare S1 at 0.20 M in a foil-wrapped reservoir to prevent premature NBS decomposition.
Prepare S2 (NBS) freshly at 0.40 M; NBS has limited solubility in CCl4 (~0.5 M at 25 °C) so 0.40 M is safely below saturation.
Purge the entire flow system with degassed CCl4 before introducing reagents.
Confirm BPR is set to 3.5 bar to keep CCl4 (bp 76.7 °C) fully liquid at 30 °C with a comfortable safety margin.
post_reactor_steps: Effluent collected into a foil-wrapped vessel to prevent further photolysis of the brominated product.
Quench with 10 wt% aqueous Na2S2O3 solution (1:1 v/v) to destroy residual NBS and neutralise HBr generated.
Separate organic layer; wash with saturated NaHCO3 then brine.
Dry over MgSO4, filter, concentrate under reduced pressure.
Purify by column chromatography (SiO2, hexane/EtOAc gradient) to isolate the beta-brominated product.
Inline IR or UV-Vis monitoring at reactor outlet recommended to track NBS consumption (NBS absorbs at ~305 nm).
proposal.chemistry_notes: The reaction is a radical alpha-bromination at the benzylic/alpha-amino acid position. NBS acts as the bromine-atom source; UV light (365 nm) initiates homolysis of the N–Br bond of NBS to generate Br•. The Boc2N-protected amino acid substrate has an activated C–H at the alpha position (benzylic + alpha to nitrogen). CCl4 is the preferred solvent because it is transparent at 365 nm, does not abstract Br• efficiently (CCl3• is less reactive toward H-abstraction than Br•), and stabilises the radical chain. The 2.0 equiv of NBS used in the batch protocol is maintained. The 70% batch yield over 8 h is expected to be matched or exceeded at 15 min residence time in flow due to (a) superior photon delivery in the thin-film annular geometry, (b) elimination of light attenuation through a bulk solution, and (c) precise temperature control. No pressure-corrected gas flow is needed as no gaseous reagent is introduced.

stage_parameters.notes: Main reaction stage; BPR downstream maintains back-pressure
Effluent depressurised to atmospheric; collected in foil-wrapped vessel

reasoning_per_field.residence_time_min: Batch reaction required 8 h in a round-bottom flask with bulk UV irradiation. In a thin-walled PFA coil (1 mm ID, ~0.5 mm wall), the optical path length is ~1 mm versus ~50 mm in a typical batch flask, improving photon flux per molecule by roughly 50×. Literature photobromination flow examples (e.g., Cantillo et al. 2014, Org. Lett.) achieve comparable conversions in 10–20 min. 15 min is chosen as a conservative estimate with a safety margin.
reasoning_per_field.flow_rate_mL_min: Total flow 0.4 mL/min (0.2 + 0.2) gives Re ~10 in 1 mm ID tubing (laminar, as expected for microflow). Reactor volume = 0.4 × 15 = 6.0 mL. This is a practical syringe-pump flow rate.
reasoning_per_field.temperature_C: Matches batch protocol (30 °C). CCl4 bp is 76.7 °C; at 3.5 bar BPR the bubble point is well above 30 °C, so single-phase liquid flow is guaranteed.
reasoning_per_field.concentration_M: Post-mix substrate concentration 0.10 M is moderate, avoiding NBS precipitation (NBS solubility in CCl4 ~0.5 M; post-mix NBS = 0.20 M, safely below limit). Batch concentration not specified; 0.10 M is a standard synthetic flow concentration.
reasoning_per_field.BPR_bar: CCl4 vapour pressure at 30 °C is ~0.15 bar. A 3.5 bar BPR provides >20× overpressure, ensuring fully liquid phase throughout. Standard BPR setting for CCl4 flow chemistry.
reasoning_per_field.reactor_type: Annular photoreactor (lamp-in-coil) maximises photon capture and minimises Beer–Lambert attenuation. PFA is UV-transparent down to ~200 nm and chemically resistant to CCl4, Br2, and HBr.
reasoning_per_field.tubing_material: PFA chosen over PTFE (opaque) and glass (fragile, harder to coil tightly). PFA transmits >90% at 365 nm for 1 mm wall thickness.
reasoning_per_field.tubing_ID_mm: 1.0 mm ID gives reactor volume of 6.0 mL at practical coil length (~7.6 m). Thin optical path ensures uniform irradiation. Larger ID would cause photon attenuation in the absorbing NBS solution.
reasoning_per_field.reactor_volume_mL: V = Q × t_R = 0.4 mL/min × 15 min = 6.0 mL. Consistent.
reasoning_per_field.wavelength_nm: NBS absorbs at 300–380 nm (n→σ* of N–Br bond). 365 nm LED sources are commercially available, energy-efficient, and monochromatic, avoiding unwanted side-photolysis of the Boc groups or the product.
reasoning_per_field.concentration_M_S1: 0.20 M in S1 reservoir; diluted 2× upon mixing with S2 to give 0.10 M in reactor.
reasoning_per_field.concentration_M_S2: 0.40 M in S2 reservoir; diluted 2× upon mixing to give 0.20 M (2.0 equiv relative to 0.10 M substrate) in reactor.

safety_flags: CCl4 is a suspected human carcinogen (IARC Group 2B) and hepatotoxin; use only in a well-ventilated fume hood or enclosed flow system with LEV. Minimise quantities by using flow (6 mL reactor vs. batch flask).
NBS is a strong oxidiser and lachrymator; handle with gloves and eye protection. Avoid contact with reducing agents.
HBr is generated as a stoichiometric by-product; ensure all fittings and BPR are HBr-compatible (PTFE/PFA/Hastelloy). Vent lines should pass through a NaOH scrubber.
UV radiation (365 nm) can cause eye and skin damage; enclose the photoreactor in an opaque housing with interlocked access panels.
CCl4 vapour pressure at 30 °C is ~150 mbar; BPR at 3.5 bar prevents boiling but any leak will release CCl4 vapour. Install a CCl4 gas detector in the enclosure.
Bromine (Br2) may be generated in trace amounts if NBS decomposes; Br2 is toxic and corrosive. The Na2S2O3 quench in post-processing destroys residual bromine species.
Radical chain reactions can be exothermic; the small thermal mass of the flow reactor and active temperature control mitigate runaway risk compared to batch.
Waste CCl4/HBr streams must be collected and disposed of as halogenated solvent waste per local regulations.
